name: Documentation Best Practices
description: This module captures the best practices for documentation, distilled from common failure modes and what tends to hold up over time.
content:
This module captures the best practices for documentation, distilled from common failure modes and what tends to hold up over time.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. State assumptions about documentation explicitly before proceeding, rather than leaving them implicit.
2. Check that documentation terminology is used consistently throughout, matching existing conventions in the surrounding context.
3. Prefer explicit, readable documentation solutions over clever ones that are hard to verify.
4. Re-check edge cases relevant to documentation (empty input, boundary values, concurrent access) before calling the task done.
5. Measure before optimizing any documentation bottleneck; do not guess at what is slow.
6. When multiple documentation strategies are viable, name the trade-off explicitly rather than silently picking one.
7. Document any non-obvious documentation decision with a short rationale so future readers understand the 'why', not just the 'what'.
8. Validate documentation outputs against a concrete example before treating the work as complete.
9. Keep documentation changes scoped to what was asked; avoid unrelated cleanup in the same pass.
10. Keep documentation outputs reproducible: fix seeds, record versions, and avoid hidden non-determinism where it matters.
11. When documentation decisions are ambiguous, favor the option that is easiest to reverse or extend later.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Do not treat a single passing example as full verification of documentation correctness.
- Do not silently drop documentation edge cases to make an example look cleaner than the real system.
- Avoid mixing unrelated documentation concerns into a single change; keep each change focused.

CLOSING NOTE
These guidelines are a starting point for documentation, not an exhaustive rulebook — use judgment when a rule doesn't fit the situation.
